#4812. Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Artists, writers, and musicians shape experience and hold the interest of an audience by introducing things that are unresolved, promise resolution, and offer hints along the way. A crime novel asks whodunnit; music creates gripping tension and aesthetic chills; plays and movies pose and ponder problems; paintings invite, and so on. Artists know that we stay with what we do not yet understand and we feel thrilled at discovery.

The journey from not knowing to understanding by way of curiosity and exploration is called an epistemic arc. Sometimes we’re captured by a puzzle and we understand gradually, sometimes the epiphany comes quickly. In either case, that aha! moment signifies the soft thump of the tiny dopamine hit that culminates an exploration. But to reach this moment, we have to be open to our existing ideas about identity and relationships being incomplete.

From the Internal Family Systems (IFS) perspective, we all have parts. We may see, hear, sense, or feel them. They present at different ages and, often, act in ways that don’t fit the current moment because they’re stuck in the past. When a part takes over and we see the world through its eyes, expecting what it expects, IFS says the part is blended. This can cause epochal (and often epical) cognitive confusion. Who am I? How old am I? Why do I think this way, feel this way, act this way? In contrast, when the part separates, or unblends, we can notice and relate to it. When we pay attention, parts unblend and we can get into relationship with them, ask what they fear, and meet their need for validation, connection, and love.

IFS therapy sessions follow the epistemic arc. Clients arrive in therapy puzzled by their behavior (Why do I pull away when I want connection?), but wedded to some familiar certainty, like I am bad, or no one can be trusted. The IFS inquiry invites them to be curious about their behavior and beliefs, which almost always leads to formative experiences.

The phenomena IFS calls blending and unblending illustrate a paradox at the heart of subjective experience. We can be a part or we can be with a part. When we are a part, we think, feel, and act like that part, but when we are with a part, we have choices. If, for example, a blended part expects rejection, we are likely to hear silence as rejection and view a later offer of help as untrustworthy or dangerous. The part is too afraid to try something new and our present remains a perpetual repetition of the past. But the opposite is true as well. If the part unblends and we are with it, we can explore its fear and challenge distorted and inaccurate beliefs. I can feel and hear a part that expects to be rejected, but since I’ll be okay whatever happens, I can afford to try something new.

An IFS session follows an epistemic arc, a process we can understand through the lens of neuroscience and predictive processing, which says the brain builds a world model in childhood and then, conserving energy, predicts the familiar. Ideally, the brain updates its predictive model in response to prediction errors, but fear and negative identity beliefs can get in the way. A person who expects rejection and withdraws will not get a chance to learn how others might respond if they were to stay present and express a need.

From the predictive processing perspective, blended parts block the brain’s ability to learn. In contrast, unblending clears the runway. IFS aims to persuade parts to unblend. Our compassion and respect invite engagement, parts acknowledge us, and mutual curiosity sustains investigation. Once parts feel valid, legitimate, lovable, and connected, we feel—and are—more open to experiences that disconfirm old beliefs. Expectations relax, other information gains influence, and the brain’s world model updates.

An IFS inquiry doesn’t push for change. Pressing a part to step aside or move quickly can confirm an expectation that its wishes and limits will be disregarded. Patience conveys concern and respect, and is valuable in itself. The message to parts is: You can hesitate and stay connected. You can express fear and be heard. IFS invites all parts to take time exploring their fears and needs. Faster? Slower? You’re the boss.

If you want to discover the logic behind some apparently inexplicable behavior of your own, encourage your parts to unblend. Try noticing them and getting curious. You might have a protective part that keeps everyone happy because it expects disagreements to end relationships. Or you might have a part that withdraws because it anticipates unreasonable—or unmeetable—demands. Your protectors can explain the rationale for their beliefs and behaviors. Your job is to listen with an open heart.

As you listen, you can validate protective choices but also challenge negative identity conclusions (I’m worthless… something is wrong with me). You can offer to replace old survival tactics with better options. You don’t have to undo the past, convince transgressors to take it back, or prove your worth. The part you protect is valid, lovable, and—if you let me help—loved. Your protectors may need to move toward this invitation slowly, starting with a question they can now tolerate asking: Can things be different? But those aha! moments, when they come, are transformative.

Schwartz, R.C. & Sweezy, M. (2020). Internal Family Systems Therapy (2nd ed.). New York NY: Guilford Press.

#4811. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4810. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4808. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4807. What Is "Emotional Regulation" for Parents?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Before I had children, I thought it would be hard and fun. I expected to be tired. I expected to have less time for myself. But I never expected to be so challenged by the emotions I had, like guilt and anger. And I was not equipped with the knowledge, skills, and tools I needed to navigate my emotions as a parent.

The emotional lives of parents are complex and important, especially for mental health. That’s because parenting evokes some of our biggest and most complicated emotions.

Having “negative” emotions towards children doesn’t mean we’re bad. It just means we have emotions, as all humans do. And contrary to what we may think, core emotions like anger, sadness, and fear are not under conscious control.

Emotional regulation refers to a calm and balanced nervous system. When we are regulated, we can experience our emotions, deal with them effectively, and relate in connected and attuned ways. When we are regulated, we don’t feel threatened by our children’s behaviors or emotions. Our capacity for compassion and curiosity is enabled—the qualities we need as parents.

Nevertheless, as parents, we are regularly thrown off balance because our children evoke strong feelings.

When I was young, I thought the only way to feel calmer was to get rid of my emotions by pushing them away or distracting myself. This is how many people think because we aren’t taught about emotions and how to be with them in healthy ways.

The goal isn’t to become a parent who never gets angry, frustrated, afraid, or overwhelmed. That’s simply not possible because emotions are hardwired into the brain and body and cannot be eradicated. Pushing emotions down dysregulates the nervous system, stressing the mind and body, which worsens anxiety and depression.

A better goal is to learn about emotions, develop emotional awareness, and ultimately learn how to process emotions. For example, being able to recognize and name the anger, fear, shame, sadness, or disappointment that you’re feeling begins the process of regulation, helping us feel and function better.

That’s a very different approach than ignoring your emotions and simply telling yourself to “calm down.”

One very effective way to understand and work with difficult emotions is through the Change Triangle, an emotional roadmap I adapted from AEDP psychotherapy and the academic literature on emotions.

Initially, the Change Triangle helps by teaching us the ABCs of emotions and how they work in the mind and body. As a result of this newfound emotional education, we can become less fearful of our emotions and more curious about what is happening inside us.

When something upsets you, you can turn inward and find where you are on the Change Triangle. You will find yourself in one of four places on the Change Triangle.

Protective defenses and inhibitory emotions obscure deeper core emotions such as anger, sadness, fear, disgust, or joy. Naming and validating our core emotions opens the door to regulation. The ultimate objective whenever we get dysregulated is to work our way back down the Change Triangle, moving from defenses back to the openhearted state of the authentic self, which is a regulated state.

Next time you get upset, instead of immediately reacting, pause and ask yourself:

This kind of curiosity creates space between feeling and action. And that space can change how we parent.

Imagine your eight-year-old refuses to turn off the television. You feel your body tighten. Your heart beats faster. You hear yourself thinking, Why won’t this kid ever listen to me?

When you listen to the anger and get curious about why you’re angry and what you need, you might notice something underneath the anger: I’m exhausted. I feel powerless. I need cooperation.

The situation hasn’t magically changed. Your child still needs to turn off the television. But now you’re responding from greater awareness rather than simply discharging the emotion.

You can set the same boundary without making your child the target of your unprocessed feelings. That’s emotional regulation.

Instead of yelling, gently take the remote from your child, turn off the TV, and tell your child calmly, “TV time is over.”

We spend enormous amounts of time teaching children about their emotions. We tell them to use their words. We teach them to take deep breaths. We encourage them to name their feelings and calm down. But parents need these skills, too. In fact, one of the most powerful ways to teach children emotional intelligence is to develop our own emotional intelligence. When parents learn to understand and process their emotions, they become better able to help their children do the same.

Damasio, A. R. (1999). The feeling of what happens: Body and emotion in the making of consciousness. Harcourt Brace.

Edler, K., & Valentino, K. (2024). Parental self-regulation and engagement in emotion socialization: A systematic review. Psychological Bulletin, 150(2), 154–191.

Fosha, D. (2000). The transforming power of affect: A model for accelerated change. Basic Books.

Hendel, H. J. (2018). It's not always depression: Working the Change Triangle to listen to the body, discover core emotions, and connect to your authentic self. Random House.

Hendel, H.J., & Fraga, J. (2025). Parents have feelings, too: A guide to navigating your emotions so you and your family can thrive. Alcove Press.

#4805. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4803. Is Psychology Measuring Introversion All Wrong?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

It used to be that if you wanted to know if someone was an introvert, you handed them a personality questionnaire, and oh, by the way, it was definitely built on the Big Five model, the dominant framework in personality science since the 1980s. Their score on the extraversion scale would have told you what you wanted to know.

But newer research is challenging the Big Five’s position as the best measure of introversion. If the critique holds, it could mean that decades of findings about introverts may have been skewed in ways I’ll explain.

The biggest problem is that the Big Five doesn’t actually measure introversion directly, which very well may mean, in effect, that it is not measuring introversion at all. You see, what the Big Five does is measure extraversion and then, believe it or not, treats introversion as the absence of extraversion. So introversion, within this model, is the low end of the extraversion dial. But that kind of makes sense, right?

Yet it paints a certain picture. A person with low extraversion is (look closely at the words I’m about to use) reserved, inhibited, quiet, or withdrawn. In the words of researchers Valerie Thomas and Pauline Nelson, the Big Five assigns “solely negative characteristics” to introverts. Oh great. Thanks. In other words, it defines introverts by what they lack rather than by the qualities and functional characteristics that they actually possess.

That’s like defining calm as “low anger,” by the way. Which would miss something essential about the experience of being calm, wouldn’t it?

So, in 2014, psychologist Jonathan Cheek and colleagues proposed the STAR Introversion Scale, measuring four distinct flavors of introversion (Cool, Jon et al., 2014):

In a 2025 study published in the Journal of Personality, Thomas and Nelson put these two approaches head-to-head, examining which better predicted solitude-seeking behavior, arguably the most signature introverted tendency (I also so argue).

Big Five introversion showed no relationship at all with positive motivation for solitude. None. Zero. Zilch. It didn’t predict wanting to be alone, and worse, under the Big Five, it was low introversion (meaning higher extraversion) that predicted actually spending more time alone. Crazy, eh? This study found that, by the Big Five’s very own logic, extraverts are the ones who are out there in the world seeking solitude for themselves, so something had clearly gone sideways.

The STAR model, on the other hand, told a coherent story about solitude. “Social introversion” predicted both the desire for and the amount of time spent alone, while curiously but understandably, “thinking introversion,” and only thinking introversion, was associated with genuinely wanting solitude, and “anxious introversion” predicted wanting solitude for negative avoidance reasons, which all makes sense to me.

When the study incorporated STAR and Big Five data and analyzed various fancy comparisons statistically, the conclusions that resulted began to indicate that perhaps where the Big Five had claimed introversion, it had actually all along been capturing something much closer to what would be better described as neuroticism. (Whoa.)

I can answer that! Well, you see, if clinical screening tools rely on Big Five-based formulations of introversion, a therapist might interpret a patient’s solitude-seeking as a symptom of a disorder rather than merely their preference. They might cast a thinking introvert who recharges alone as socially withdrawn. Alternatively, they might underestimate the functional impact of an anxious introvert’s distress given that it’s literally part of a normalized trait score, when in fact, it is an indication of clinically concerning functioning and treatable patterns. Ah, you see now?

In workplaces, the Big Five framework feeds a narrative in which introversion is a deficit to be managed, such as the stereotypical quiet employee who needs to “come out of their shell.” In reality, there is not necessarily a defensive shell at all but, rather, likely a vital interior life. Such confusion risks a perpetuation in varying forms and degrees of, in effect, pathologizing perfectly functional ways of being human.

To me, the STAR’s great contribution is carving out space for thinking introversion, a dimension completely invisible to the Big Five, for introverts who don’t avoid people out of anxiety but do also gravitate toward ideas, reflection, imagination, and, thus, toward solitude. This is arguably at the heart of what most self-identified introverts mean when they say “introvert” to describe themselves (can I get an amen?).

But still, clearly the STAR model has its own vulnerabilities. It is relatively new, developed by a small research group, and has had as-yet-limited independent validation across diverse populations (equity!). And “anxious introversion” is easily debatable. If it so strongly correlates with neuroticism, is it even an aspect of introversion, or is it really something altogether different, albeit related, that should be measured separately?

Whatever the case on the nuances, it is clear enough that the STAR is bringing a serious challenge to whether the Big Five, for all its strengths, has introversion right.

As I’ve alluded, emerging evidence suggests it does not—that it has been measuring only a shadow of introversion, defined by deficit and tinged with pathology, while missing the fuller, more textured reality, so I am appreciative of new perspectives.

This new conversation is just beginning, but for the many millions (including myself, hi) who have long felt that their introversion is something richer than “not extraverted enough,” the science may thankfully, finally, hopefully, be catching up.

Cheek, J. M., Brown, C. A., & Grimes, J. O. (2014). Personality scales for four domains of introversion: Social, thinking, anxious, and restrained introversion. Unpublished manuscript, Department of Psychology, Wellesley College. (The original STAR Introversion Scale.)

Thomas, V., & Nelson, P. A. (2025). The effects of multifaceted introversion and sensory processing sensitivity on solitude-seeking behavior. Journal of Personality. (Head-to-head comparison of the STAR and the Big Five Inventory in predicting solitude-seeking; source of the finding that Big Five introversion fails to predict positive motivation for solitude.)

#4800. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4798. Why Reconciliation Fails (and What Actually Makes It Work)

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

It seems family estrangement is showing up everywhere lately on social media. In particular, we see numerous headlines of adult children going “no contact." And, to some extent, the statistics support this observation.

A 2024 Harris Poll showed about half of American adults are estranged from at least one close relative, with 35 percent estranged from an immediate family member, such as a parent or sibling. Cornell sociologist Karl Pillemer estimates that 67 million Americans are estranged and that more than 4 in 10 will experience it at some point in their lives.

With this growing reality, reconnection often becomes a focus for one or both parties after estrangement, raising two very important questions. Firstly, why does family reconciliation so often break down, and secondly, what helps reconciliation succeed?

If you're estranged and searching for a way to reconnect, you may be feeling and carrying around a particular type of hope. Despite previous unsuccessful attempts to close the gap, you picture it going differently this time. You work to convince yourself that if you could only find the right words, everything would be fixed. But it isn’t.

After more than a decade of working in this field, I've discovered that words might not matter as much as we think they do. What actually determines how these conversations go is whether two people can stay emotionally present when words start to hurt, and to stay open, as opposed to shutting down or exchanging salvos, when things get tough.

What I see is that when one person describes your behavior in a way that’s painful to hear, you feel discomfort. In many cases, your body reacts instantly, before your mind has a chance to process the words. The other person hasn’t even finished their sentence, and you're already overwhelmed with the urge to respond, in all likelihood, with a counterattack. And most of the time, it doesn't feel like defensiveness from the inside. It probably feels like protecting yourself.

However, for the person who has worked up the courage to say the hard, painful thing, the message becomes that being honest isn't safe. And, therefore, the relationship isn't safe. And, until it is, repair cannot happen.

This is where I see many reconciliation attempts falter and stall. The fact that it’s even attempted underscores something incredibly important. Someone cares enough to give it a try. The unfortunate reality is that the well-intentioned bid for reconnection fails because of an inability to hear the other’s experience without the need to defend, deny, or deflect. This is at the heart of the problem. Only when it’s recognized and addressed can a space for genuine reconnection be created.

Let me give you an example. A woman had chosen estrangement from her mother. Over time, her mother would reach out periodically. Each time, conversations started like an apology but quickly disintegrated into explanations that felt like justifications. Recollections only accommodated one set of experiences, the mother’s. Following each conversation, the daughter felt like nothing had changed. Each failed attempt increased the gap even further.

In order to make sense of this recurring pattern, the daughter turned to therapy and, through that process, became aware that she’d allowed her own healing to become dependent on a mother who might never want to or be able to hear her in the way she needed.

She longed for her mother to listen, acknowledge her childhood experiences, and take responsibility. But, repeatedly, that craved-for moment remained painfully elusive. So, she decided to stop waiting for something external that might never come and started healing anyway.

When the next reconnection attempt eventually happened, there was little to no expectation. Once she let go of needing her mother to own the past, things changed. She still received the same excuses, and the defensiveness remained, but now the daughter viewed both in a different light. She saw armor that had always been there. Armor that, importantly, she came to realise, had nothing to do with her.

In reality, the relationship remained far from what the daughter really longed for. For years, she’d hoped her mother would turn up to the conversation without armor and had weighted her expectations accordingly. Ultimately, it had become clear to her that her mother might never be capable of staying emotionally present and open. The only way to break the deadlock was to be a different daughter.

In making that decision, she and her mother embarked on a new relationship, one where she had created her own conditions for safety. One where she was emotionally present and open, and where, little by little, repair became possible.

Strangely, this isn't unusual. Research from the Family Estrangement & Reconciliation Project found this pattern spanning hundreds of successful reconciliations. Often, the people who rebuilt their relationships weren't the ones who finally got the listening, recognition, and understanding they'd been waiting for. They were the ones who embraced the importance of letting go of never-to-be-met expectations from an irreconcilable shared past.

So, on one hand, reconciliation could be seen as an attempt to reclaim and redirect the past. On the other hand, it can also become the foundation for something new and different. And, with the latter of these two possibilities, it doesn’t mean saying everything that happened in the past was fine. Nor does it mean that one’s experiences are unimportant. It simply means that one can finally put down things that should never been carried in the first place, so that healing and growth can happen.

I don't talk about this from theory alone. I have been estranged from a parent myself. I know how long the road back to rebuilding a stable relationship can be.

It might seem counterintuitive, but wherever you are in your journey, travel as lightly as possible. Carry fewer expectations, explanations, and justifications. Before ever considering the words you might use to try and bridge the gap between you and an estranged loved one, take a look at what you’re bringing with you.

To what extent the other person meets you halfway is largely beyond your control. That said, turning up to the conversation armed with a deeper degree of self-awareness, emotional grounding, and a commitment to healing that isn’t conditional on what the other person does or doesn’t do can often bring reconciliation within reach.

#4797. I’ve Hiked All 7 Continents—This Is the Cold-Weather Boot I Recommend for Winter Treks

And more winter hiking gear we pack for every cold trek.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WE’RE HALFWAY THROUGH fall (seriously?!), and that means winter is just around the corner. Colder weather and—depending on where you live and hike—snow, freezing rain, ice, and sleet are all very real possibilities on the trail in the coming months. It’s time to pack away most of your three-season hiking gear and bust out your dedicated cold-weather kit.

Prepping for winter hiking is all about staying dry, warm, and comfortable. Whether you’re looking to upgrade your current outerwear—everything from jackets and hats to hiking boots and socks—or this is your first winter hiking season, we’ve rounded up the best cold-weather hiking gear to help you tackle the trail this year. As a seasoned hiker who’s explored all seven continents over the last 30 years, this is what I recommend in 2026.

Rugged, weatherproof, and ready for the nastiest winter conditions, this new-for-2026 boot is one winter hiking boot to rule them all. But, don’t let the chunky design fool you. These are among the most comfortable, streamlined cold-weather kicks I’ve ever worn (weighing 17.5 ounces), making them versatile enough for not only winter, but challenging shoulder season hikes too.

Like most everything in Paka’s lineup, the Sol Crew leans on a combination of synthetic and natural fibers, giving you the best of both worlds. The Tencel-meets-alpaca construction is breathable, quick-wicking, and extremely odor-resistant. It feels great against the skin as a true base layer, and the dash of Spandex adds just the right amount of stretch. Plus, it’s versatile enough to double as a sun shirt in warmer weather with UPF 30+ sun protection.

If I had to pick just one favorite Mountain Hardwear jacket, the new go-to StretchDown Jacket gets the nod. It’s warm, packable, durable, and the stretch gives it an edge over most other down jackets, with the athletic fit stretching to accommodate beefier layers in deep cold weather. That’s gotten even better with the latest update to the baffling with DoppleWeave, which catches more down and keeps it from migrating much less—making for less cold spots. Plus, it’s available in Light, Medium, and Big “weights,” so you can dial in the exact warmth level that suits your hiking style.

I’ve worn Mammut’s Runbold IV hiking pants on three continents and they’ve never let me down. This winter-ready version is just as wind-resistant and water-repellent, but the addition of a light fleece liner adds even more comfort and a just-right level of warmth. Three zippered pockets add plenty of storage options, and mesh-lined zippered vents keep you from overheating on the trail. Bonus: It’s all made with eco-friendly, bluesign-certified materials.

Keeping your feet dry at all costs is doubly important in winter when unpredictable conditions can deliver freezing rain, ice, snow, or some combination of all three. These socks are phenomenal in wet, cold weather, making them invaluable for winter hiking. They're like wearing a wetsuit bootie on your feet (except with no hinderance in range of motion).

Smartwool’s soft, natural, Merino-centric collection has been a favorite of mine for more than a decade. This OG base layer offers a more relaxed fit (compared to the suctioned-to-the-body vibe of most thermals) and a midweight warmth that’s perfect for layering under hiking pants, ski pants, or just about any cold-weather bottoms. Plus, Smartwool’s is among the softest Merino on the market.

The two-piece design adds a rolltop outer sleeve to a traditional HydraPak water bladder. The result is a setup that’s designed to keep cold water cold in the summer, but with the added benefit of keeping warm water warm for winter hikes. It also helps ensure that your water supply doesn’t straight-up freeze in deep cold conditions.

I’ve been a fan of Icebreaker’s RealFleece blend for years—it’s softer and more luxurious than traditional wool but with all the benefits of natural Merino. This midweight top makes this the perfect in-between top that layers well (on top or underneath) in colder weather. The half-zip design is also great for quickly dumping heat on the go.

The OG Buff is arguably the most versatile piece of apparel in my pack. This winter-ready version upgrades to Polartec fleece that’s warm, buttery soft, and fast-drying. The stretchy construction allows for wearing it any of ten different ways, and UPF 50 protection shields your neck and face on harsh sunny days.

I appreciate a pair of midweight gloves that balances reliable warmth and weather resistance with enough dexterity to allow me to still use my phone, camera, and do the things that heavyweight ski gloves often make impossible on the trail. The Denali checks all of these boxes while adding a silicone grip and touchscreen-friendly fingertips to boot.

Arc’teryx’s Bird Head Toque brings a dash of understated cool to winter hiking headgear, and is amongst the most popular beanies you’ll find right now. I love the oversized classic “dinosaur bird” logo and bold color options. And the blended Merino/acrylic construction ensures that it’s soft, warm, quick-drying, and moisture-wicking—perfect for long winter days on the trail.

Fancy rainshells can be obscenely expensive. Spyder takes most of the next-gen technical features of the best shells I’ve personally tested—four-way stretch, solid DWR, and excellent breathability—and packages them into the surprisingly affordable Clutch that’s available for under $200. Bonus: It ditches the “crinkly plastic bag” vibe of most other rain shells, keeping you quieter on the trail.

Hyperlite leans heavy on next-gen Dyneema Woven Composite 3.9 fabric, ensuring the Southwest 40 is lightweight, extremely durable, and completely weatherproof—all essential for intense winter hikes. I love the roll-top design that keeps things dead simple with just the right amount of organization and nothing more. (I also like that it’s available in 55L and 70L variations for longer expeditions.)

All modern hiking apparel is made from natural fibers, synthetic fibers, or a blend of the two. Merino and alpaca wool are my two favorite natural options, as both offer excellent thermal regulation, breathability, and odor-resistance. They’re fantastic for longer trips, allowing you to pack less and travel farther while staying dry, comfortable, and stink-free. In most cases, however, they tend to be more expensive than their synthetic counterparts.

Synthetic fibers like polyester, nylon, and polypropylene all dry faster than Merino, are typically lighter weight, and more budget-friendly. However, they don’t offer the same odor resistance, and they’re all petroleum-based products. So, they’re hardly eco-friendly.

The key is regulating your body temperature with proper layering. Start with a thin base layer that feels good against the skin and fits closely without being too restrictive. Add an insulating midlayer like a half-zip or full-zip fleece. In especially cold conditions, adding a down shirt or full down jacket will help provide extra warmth. Top it off with a final layer that’s designed for weather protection (to fend off wind and precipitation) in the form of a hard or soft shell. Gore-Tex is the gold standard for this last layer as it offers the best protection, however, it’s also the most expensive. To maintain a comfortable body temperature and ensure you don’t overheat (and sweat), shed or add layers as necessary throughout your cold weather hike. This is where having a little extra room in your pack allows for stashing those extra layers.

There are a lot of individual factors that determine which jacket is right for you, including the quality of down used and how cold or hot you tend to run personally. But fill power is often the most straightforward spec to consider when determining the warmth of a puffy or down jacket. In general, 700 to 800 fill power will keep you warm for most cold-weather hikes. Upgrade to 850-plus fill power for extreme, subzero winter conditions.

It’s also important to consider the face fabric construction. Denier measures both weight and durability. For example, a 7D to 10D down jacket will be lighter and more packable, but also more prone to damage on the trail. Upgrading to a 15D-plus puffer adds weight but also durability. There’s no right answer as it depends on your budget and style of hiking.

Boot insulation is often measured in grams. A winter hiking boot with 200 grams of insulation should suffice in most cold weather conditions, while a 400g+ alternative is better for subzero temps, hiking in snow, or if your feet run cold. A waterproof membrane (again, Gore-Tex is best) is essential for winter boots, especially if you know you’ll be hiking in wet or snowy conditions. Finally, look for an outsole with a winter-centric tread compound with multi-directional lugs (I love Vibram Arctic Grip) for maximum traction in snow and ice.

As an avid hiker and adventure travel writer for more than two decades, I've tested countless outdoor products from all of the world's most recognized brands. Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and his own personal testing in the winter months.

While testing cold weather hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, warmth, ease of packing, weight, durability, functionality, performance, and necessity.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

#4796. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

Heatpumps over here have been able to do this for years already.

And it's not one of two signals. Inverter controlled HP's enables control of the effect, and not just "normal or boost".

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4795. What Young Adults Want Parents to Know About Them

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I am a psychologist who helps to run an Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) for young adults ages 18-26. These young people are facing mental health challenges that temporarily prevent them from enjoying their lives and relationships to the fullest extent they might. They also may be struggling with independence, as well as career or college progression. Here are some of the themes that I have heard consistently over the past few years. I hope it helps you to connect with and support your young adult children.

I do care about my future. If I am taking a leave of absence from college or am struggling with keeping or finding a job, it is not because I do not care. I care very much, actually. However, I am struggling with anxiety, depression, or other mental health concerns that need to be addressed before I can resume my journey.

I may not always like you, but I do love you. We have spent a lot of time together over the years, and it has not always been easy. In fact, we may disagree about a lot of things. However, that does not mean that I do not love you. Yes, I can not like you at times and still love you. Please remember that.

I want you to listen and see me for who I am. My personality and values are very important to me. I may not have everything figured out yet, and I am still learning about myself and the world, but I ask that you respect me for who I am today. Ask questions and be curious about what is important to me. If you ask in an open, loving way, I am happy to let you into my world.

I am frightened of the future, so please do not minimize the state of the world I am inheriting. Let’s be honest, the older generations have not left us with a world that is thriving and well. Selfish politicians, wars, climate change — all of this is stressful to me. So, yes, I have lost faith in “the system.” And can you blame me? Please be sympathetic when I am discouraged about the state of the world.

The world is different now than it was when you were my age (and not in a good way). It is a difficult time to be a young adult. With the introduction of AI and the comparisons on social media, life is particularly stressful for me. Yes, you had your own stressors, but please know that what we are dealing with now is new territory. No one knows where it will lead, which is stressful and scary for me.

Online friends are real friends too. I know you may not understand because the world is different today, but connecting with others online can be meaningful too. Especially while living through the pandemic, we had to get creative in how we meet and interact with others. Sometimes online connection feels safer and easier, actually.

Please, never give up on me. I know I am going through a difficult time. I may be struggling with my next steps academically, professionally, or personally. That does not mean that I have failed or that I will struggle my whole life. I just need some help and support now. I am excited for what is next but may need to heal and regroup first. Please stay in my corner as I prepare for what’s next.
