#4794. The 91 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 14 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4793. Cadillac’s most affordable EV just got a bit cheaper

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range, a massive 33″ infotainment screen, an NACS charge port, and now it’s a bit more affordable.

The Optiq first went on sale in 2025 as Cadillac’s entry-level electric SUV, starting at $54,390. For the 2026 model year, the Optiq arrived as GM’s first electric vehicle with a built-in NACS port and added a new rear-wheel-drive (RWD) powertrain.

Thanks to the new RWD option, the 2026 Optiq (see our review) was also slightly less expensive, with prices starting at $52,395.

While GM initially said the 2027 Cadillac Optiq would start at $52,695, prices on its website have been updated and are now slightly lower.

The base 2027 Cadillac Optiq Luxury RWD is now listed at $51,790, or $905 less than the initial price announced months ago. The Luxury AWD trim is also $905 cheaper, starting at $55,290.

Meanwhile, the Sport trim now starts at $52,395 for RWD and $55,895 for AWD, both $900 less than before.

The higher-spec Optiq Premium Luxury, Premium Sport, and V-Series trims remain at the price GM initially announced.

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range in the RWD models and 303 miles with AWD. All models come with a standard 33″ Horizon Display infotainment screen, a 19-speaker AKG Studio Audio System, GM’s Super Cruise hands-free driver-assist technology, and a native NACS charge port.

Upgrading to AWD costs an extra $3,500. The Premium Luxury and Premium Sport add standard features including a Head-Up Display, ventilated and lumbar massaging front seats, and a rear cargo cover.

The high-performance 2027 Optiq-V starts at $69,295 and delivers a Cadillac-estimated 519 lb-ft of torque and 650 horsepower in Velocity MaX Mode,

How does the Cadillac Optiq stack up against the Tesla Model Y? The base Tesla Model Y RWD starts at $39,990 with up to 321 miles of range, while the AWD version costs $41,990 and gets up to 294 miles.

The Tesla Model Y Premium RWD starts at $45,990 with up to 355 miles of range, while the Premium AWD starts at $49,990 and has 327 miles of range.

Had the opportunity to drive the Optiq as a loaner while my Lyriq was in for service. I truly liked how it handled but I did find what I call a safety issue due to its design. The A pillar has an extra vertical piece and that combined with really no usable visual space forward and the side mirror create a blind spot when wanting to make a left turn on dark roads. No problem in the city where there is light. If GM would have added front side lighting when making a turn that could have been eliminated. Would have seriously looked at the Optiq for the next vehicle but that blind spot is a show stopper for me. Well that, and the fact the Optiq does not support CarPlay.

Inside, the base Tesla Model Y has a 16″ QHD touchscreen and 7-speaker audio system. The Premium model gains a 15-speaker Tesla Audio System with a subwoofer, plus an 8″ second-row touchscreen.

The two are nearly the same size, but the Tesla Model Y offers slightly more rear legroom and cargo capacity than the Cadillac Optiq.

#4792. Why One Good Thing Leads to Another

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

After reading the responses to my last post about the art of asking questions, in which I described the importance of becoming better listeners to ensure more meaningful connection with others, I’ve been thinking about something else: how one small action can set other good things in motion.

Here’s what got me thinking. A woman from a media company that uses puppets to teach elementary-school children important skills reached out. She was so excited about the idea of teaching genuine curiosity to young people that she is talking with her staff about creating episodes on asking interesting questions.

She wrote: I'm part of the team behind Sunnyside Roadshow, a daily, five-minute social-emotional learning program for elementary school children that uses puppetry, storytelling, and humor to help develop important life skills.

"As I read your article, I found myself wondering: Can we begin teaching children, at an early age, the art of being genuinely curious about other people? Kids are naturally eager to share their own experiences, and understandably so! But could we help them learn to pause, listen, ask another question, and show interest in what someone else is saying?

…Rather than simply teaching children not to interrupt and act on impulse, what if we could help them discover the joy of being genuinely interested in another person's experiences? Could we intentionally model curiosity through our characters' conversations, showing children how asking one thoughtful follow-up question can make someone feel heard and valued? If they worked on these skills together in the classroom, wouldn't we help raise more thoughtful humans?"

A post about ways to deepen conversation through becoming better listeners might lead to children learning how to show interest in others. Those children could bring that curiosity to their friendships, their families, and eventually their adult relationships. We have no way of knowing how far those ripples might travel.

Other people wrote that the post prompted them to reflect on their own conversational habits. They recognized themselves in the tendency to tell stories and talk about themselves rather than ask questions, and vowed to be more inquisitive.

That’s how it starts. Someone does something. Someone else responds. And on and on.

And it doesn’t require writing a post or creating a children’s program.

Think about the times you checked out at Trader Joe’s and were asked, “What are your plans for today?” or “Got anything fun planned this weekend?” For some customers, that might be the only conversation they have all day. What seems like a casual question can be a moment of genuine connection. And think about the difference that brief connection might make—not only for the person leaving the store, but also for the people they encounter throughout the day.

A few months ago, as I was checking out of Trader Joe’s, a clerk asked me about my plans, and I mentioned that I was having a party.

He ran off and returned with a gorgeous bouquet of flowers—all my favorite colors. He had no idea how much that unexpected kindness meant to me. And now, months later, I’m telling you about it. His gesture is still traveling.

My mother understood something about this, too. A New Yorker, she would often pay the toll for a complete stranger in the car behind her when crossing the George Washington Bridge.

Imagine pulling up to the tollbooth, reaching for your money, and being told that someone had already paid. Someone you didn’t know and probably would never meet. I loved that about her.

Did those drivers go on to do something kind for someone else? I don’t know. But my mother’s gestures stayed with me. That, too, is a ripple.

We often think that making a difference requires a grand plan, lots of time, or something extraordinary to offer. Meanwhile, we overlook the opportunities right in front of us: asking a question and truly listening to the answer, offering a sincere compliment, including someone who seems left out, or letting someone know that something they did mattered.

So here’s my challenge: Do one small thing today that might set other good things in motion.

Treat it as an experiment. Notice what happens—to the other person and to you. You may see an immediate response, or you may never know where your gesture leads.

Either way, tip over that first domino. And watch the fun begin.

And if the spirit moves you, email me and tell me what happened. I’d love to hear.

#4791. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4790. The 60 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#4789. Hardee’s gets EV fast charging – with Carl’s Jr. locations to follow

EV drivers have a new reason to pull into Hardee’s. Energized EV has opened four fast-charging ports at a restaurant in Temple, Georgia, kicking off a planned rollout at Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. locations across the US.

There’s no site count or rollout schedule yet, but the first location is open with both NACS and CCS1 connectors.

The chargers are at 587 Carrollton Street in Temple. The site has two dual-port XCharge C7 DC fast chargers, each rated at 240 kW, for a total of four charging ports. Monta provides the chargers’ software. XCharge says the C7 adjusts power output between its two connectors, and both NACS and CCS1 connectors are on offer.

“Adding charging at our restaurants gives EV drivers a convenient place to stop, recharge, and enjoy a meal,” said Mike Darger, vice president of facilities and maintenance at CKE Restaurants. “We look forward to building on this first opening as more locations come online across the country.”

Energized EV says more Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. sites are planned across the US, with president and CEO Devin Grandis calling Temple “the beginning of a much larger expansion.”

Energy & Environmental Design Services LLC (E&EDS) is the program’s exclusive installer. Its services include charging infrastructure design, installation, and maintenance, as well as electrical contracting.

Yes. I love this. As in past comments sections on stories like this, the question comes up for me as to how they manage them. Will people eating there use them or will they become a "charging stop" that drivers use often? Then there's the saga of how to keep the lazy and over-sized patrons from parking their 2004 Explorer in those spaces.

Gas stations with food offered and restaurants with charging offered are similar yet different. Instead of eating while you gas up, we can now charge up while we eat. The latter being the better option.

Energized EV’s approach is to install chargers where drivers already stop, whether they’re running errands or taking a longer road trip. But we’ll need the next locations and opening dates to see how useful this restaurant charging network will become. The announcement doesn’t list charging prices for Temple.

#4788. Why We Love Talking Animals

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

From Aesop to Orwell, from the Three Little Pigs to Bugs Bunny, our stories are full of talking animals. Foxes flatter, lions boast, and donkeys mope. For thousands of years, we have used animals to tell stories about ourselves.

But why use animals? Why not just use people?

Consider this short tale by the ancient Greek fabulist Aesop, The Fox and the Mask:

A fox broke into the house of an actor and noticed a mask in the midst of a pile of stage accessories. The fox dragged out the mask and nuzzled and swatted it for a few moments, before saying, “What a handsome face, pity he has no brains.”

Or consider this fable from the Ancient Indian Panchatantra, in which a rabbit outwits a lion:

A lion was terrorising the animals of the jungle, killing far more than he could eat. To appease him, the animals agreed that, each day, they would send him one of their number. When a rabbit’s turn came, he arrived late, telling the lion that another lion had kept him by claiming to be the true king of the jungle. Enraged, the lion demanded to see this imposter. The rabbit led him to a well, in which the lion saw his own reflection. Mistaking it for his rival, he leapt in and drowned.

The use of animals creates new and striking possibilities. It stokes the imagination, making the tale seem more original and entertaining, even charming, without which it might fall flat as moralising or patronising. We are more willing to listen to a fox than to a preacher, and more likely to remember what it has to say.

The use of animals also enables the storyteller to isolate a vice and caricature it, while at the same time providing a fresh perspective on it. Each animal becomes a shorthand for a particular human vice or trait. We are often resistant to criticism, especially when it concerns our character. But when we laugh at a vain crow or a pessimistic donkey, we may be laughing at ourselves. The animal creates a certain psychological distance, enabling us to recognise our faults without feeling accused and becoming defensive.

On a deeper level, talking animals create a continuum between human and animal, revealing us as part of nature and at one with it, while also highlighting what sets us apart from the rest of creation, namely, speech and reason (Greek, logos) and the capacity for moral reflection.

As I discuss in The Meaning of Myth, animals appeal especially to children, possibly because blurring the lines between human and animal is a form of pre-logical, magical thinking. Children readily attribute thoughts, feelings, and intentions to animals, and may find a talking rabbit or bear no more extraordinary than a talking human. For adults, the attraction is more subtle: the talking animal offers both an escape from reality and a means of understanding it, in particular, through the pleasure of analogising.

Finally, the use of animals can serve as a cover, a means of escaping censorship, or of generalising or universalising. Jean de La Fontaine (d. 1695) used the fable form to satirise French society, and George Orwell used it to satirise communism and other forms of totalitarianism, while also making us smile.

Animals delight us still today, every day, if only in cartoons and viral videos, because, as the fabulist might say, “So it is with men, too.”

You may also enjoy my companion piece, The Symbolism of Snakes.

#4787. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

#4786. The BMW iX is sold out, but you might like what takes its place even more

BMW is saying goodbye to the iX. With the 2026 model essentially sold out, BMW is preparing to introduce its replacement, which already looks like a big upgrade.

The iX went on sale in the US in 2022 as BMW’s first dedicated electric SUV. After a short four-year run, BMW confirmed earlier this year that it was discontinuing the iX in the US after the 2026 model year to make room for its next-generation of fully electric vehicles.

BMW didn’t take long to sell through inventory, with 2026 iX models essentially sold out in the US.

The iX landing page now redirects you to the new BMW X5 instead. According to online auto research firm CarsDirect, about 10 new iX models remain nationwide.

BMW’s Neue Klasse vehicles, starting with the new 2027 iX3, mark a step change from its previous EVs.

At the center is the Neue Klasse platform, which introduces BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, new batteries, and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

BMW said the new Gen6 eDrive system delivers 30% higher charging speeds and driving range than its previous system, with some models seeing an even greater increase.

The 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle, starts at $61,500 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles. In comparison, the 2026 iX xDrive 60 had an EPA range of up to 364 miles.

While the iX3 is a smaller, compact electric SUV compared to the iX, BMW is preparing to launch the iX5 as a more direct replacement.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now on sale, starting at $72,100, but BMW is expected to launch the electric iX5 in early 2027.

A few weeks ago, BMW put the new iX5 60 xDrive to the test at an international media event in Southern California to show just how fast it can charge.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW. BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to an estimated 435 miles of range on a single charge.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 will be an upgrade from the iX, adopting BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The setup includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the windshield. You can also opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

The new drive platform is a huge improvement. Personally I'm glad to see it in the new i3 since I don't think everyone needs a 3-ton SUV.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, the iX5 is slightly longer and taller than the outgoing iX, with more of a traditional SUV design.

BMW is expected to open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive this month, starting at $79,800, with a full launch in early 2027. It will be BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US.

Production is set to begin at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year, with the first deliveries expected in early 2027.

#4785. Reading as a Green Flag Is a Dating Trend

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Are you looking to date someone who's on the same page with you? Or how about on any page—as in, does the person actually read things like books and not just social media posts? Well, you may have read about how reading has become a prominent green flag—meaning that many people are actively looking for it on dating profiles and dates.

For example, after pop star Dua Lipa married actor Callum Turner, many fans seemed to get excited about the cover version, so to speak, of their meet-cute, as described by an article by Ellen Durney for Buzzfeed. Turner indicated that they had first met at a mutual friend’s birthday party and soon realized that they were both reading the book Trust by Hernán Díaz and were even on the same chapter. This apparently helped them trust each other more, with Turner claiming that he had told Lipa then, “So we’re on the same page.” And that, kids, is how Dua became a duo.

These days, whether someone reads, period, can be a dating screening criterion, depending on where you stand on this whole reading thing. That's because there is a big reading divide in the U.S. For example, the Pew Research Center found that nearly a quarter (~23%) of Americans surveyed didn't even touch a book over the past 12 months. In fact, the National Endowment for the Arts and American Time Use Survey have shown that only 16% or so of Americans may be reading on a daily basis, and over 51% may be reading absolutely no books each year.

Social media may be making this divide more obvious. Just look at how many times someone posts an opinion and the response is something like "Have you even read about this?" or even "Did you even read the link that you posted?" So, if you do fall on the regularly reading side of the divide, it might make sense to have regular reading as a minimal dating requirement.

But it could go even beyond that. The reading app Headway found in a survey that ”Some 24% of people instantly swipe right on dating profiles that show someone reading, while 75% prefer a partner who is well-read over someone physically attractive." Yep, reading could even be, gasp, sexy. That might have been a War and Peace of news to you in high school, when it seemed like all that people were interested in was looks.

But if you think about it, regularly reading stuff that's more than just cereal boxes and messages with ROFL in them can tell a lot about a person. It could suggest that the person is intellectually curious, willing to learn, and more thoughtful and mindful. There is also the standard saying that the brain is the biggest and most powerful sexual organ. The size of a person's creativity, empathy, and knowledge could play a bigger role in pleasing a partner than the size of anything else. And if you are looking for, umm, enhancement in all those areas, reading can be at your service.

Once you find someone who actually reads regularly—assuming that's what you want, since you have already gotten this far on this article—it can also help to find out what, specifically, the person reads. What someone reads can tell you a whole lot more about a person than the person's photo. That's because reading is something that takes time and effort and is done on one's own time.

So, those who will dedicate their time to reading about something are likely interested in that thing at least to some degree. For example, anyone who has read a lot of books about cats probably likes cats. Or, maybe, is preparing for the big cat government overthrow that will eventually occur. Either way, that person likely has a more informed opinion about cats.

Someone's reading materials can also be a clue to that person's point of view. Guess what reading "Surrounded by Idiots" may say about a person's current life situation. Also, the diversity of their reading materials could reflect their diversity of thought and perspectives and their open-mindedness.

All of this can be important information since a big part of dating is finding the right match in terms of personality, values, and other core qualities. A person's reading list doesn't necessarily say everything about someone. For example, when I was doing research to write an article about farts, I was reading a lot about farts. But I am more than farts. Nevertheless, reading lists can be another clue to help you read someone better.

There's a lot to be read about using reading to help gauge people, but also, to meet people in the first place. Eventbrite data did show a 33% increase in book club events in the first half of 2026. Such data also showed that the number "romantasy" events around the U.S. have gone up by 196% in 2026 compared to 2025, with attendance jumping by 237%. A "romantasy event" is a gathering that's built around the whole romantic fantasy literary genre. This is fiction that brings together mystical worlds and romantic plots.

For example, there was the three-day Romantasy BookCon in Orlando, Florida, in October. There was cosplay, author appearances, and book signings, and a variety of ways lovers of this genre could mix together. Now, while the focus of that event was not dating, who knows what can happen when lovers of the same thing come together. They might end up becoming lovers of lovers of that thing.

All of this does not mean that you should pretend to like reading when you don't. People trying to be what they are not is a big reason why there are so many mismatches and bad relationships out there. But it does mean that if you do things by the book regularly, this could end up being the book on love for you.

#4784. The 6 Best Adjustable Kettlebells, Tested by Editors and Certified Trainers

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

These offerings from REP Fitness and Bells of Steel are some of the best.

KETTLEBELLS OFFER PLENTY of bang for your buck. You can use them for strength training, muscle building, and explosive movements like snatches and swings. You can achieve all of this with just one kettlebell, making it a tool that’s as simple as it is effective. Not only that, but they are actually fun to use; I've put together plenty of grueling workouts with kettlebells that had me grinning from ear to ear at the end.

If you want to get stronger, you’ll need a heavier kettlebell, and buying multiple bells can get pricey. Our favorite solution is the adjustable kettlebell, which, like the best adjustable dumbbells and the best weighted vests, is a highly versatile piece of equipment. Our editors researched and tested the most popular—and even lesser-known—adjustable kettlebells to find the six best to get for your home gym.

Our guide is competitive. Many iconic brands produce adjustable kettlebells with rave reviews and similar specs. What puts REP’s adjustable kettlebell in our Best Overall spot is that it looks, feels, and performs most like a standard kettlebell—even the handle diameter is nearly competition-grade—and the price is very fair for the equipment you’re getting.

Like nearly everything REP produces, this kettlebell sets the standard for quality. The frame is cast iron and powder-coated to improve grip. The traditional shape lets kettlebell athletes use it, so their training transfers to competition. Even the bottom of the kettlebell is covered in rubber to protect your floor—a minor detail we appreciate. Typically, you’re paying above market for this level of quality and design, but REP’s adjustable kettlebell is less expensive than other picks here.

REP offers three different weight ranges: 8-16kg (17-35lbs), 16-24kg (35-53lbs), and 10-40lbs. The kilogram kettlebells adjust in two-kilogram increments, and the pound kettlebells adjust in five-pound increments. To select your weight, turn the dial on top of the kettlebell (below the handle). Then lift the kettlebell off the weight stack, where the remaining plates will sit for the duration of your set or workout.

If you want to nitpick, other brands have said that the plastic dial feels cheap and prone to breaking. We want to highlight this detail, but our editors don’t think this is an issue unless you plan on abusing the kettlebell.

No matter which weight range you choose, you’re replacing five kettlebells. For general fitness enthusiasts, we like the 10- 40 lb option; it’s enough weight to challenge you for presses and high-rep sets of squats and rows. If you have some lifting experience and want to primarily train explosive movements like swings and snatches, as you traditionally do with kettlebells, opt for the 16-24 kg range. Unless you’re a complete beginner, we suggest those two weight ranges.

Bells of Steel created something very cool with this competition-spec adjustable kettlebell. The weight range and increments are fantastic, and the dimensions match competition specs exactly. You’ll replace 18 kettlebells for less than $300. Two reasons it’s not our overall best pick are that the adjustment process is comparatively time-consuming, and a competition-style bell isn’t for everyone.

To change the weights of the Bells of Steel kettlebell, you need a few minutes and a couple of tools. Use an Allen wrench to undo the bolt on the bottom of the kettlebell, remove the bottom half, then loosen the other screw that secures the plates with a traditional wrench. You can then add more plates in half-kilogram increments to the bolt that runs through the top half of the shell. Because the adjustment process is more time-consuming, this isn’t the best kettlebell for circuits or workouts that demand you change weights on the fly.

At first glance, you probably can’t even tell this is an adjustable kettlebell; it has a smooth cast-iron finish, no dials or switches, and a 35-millimeter handle that looks identical to standard competition kettlebells. This adjustable kettlebell is for serious kettlebell athletes. That said, if you’ve never trained with an adjustable kettlebell, be aware that the stainless steel handle can rub the hand raw (use a lot of chalk), it’ll feel more cumbersome than other picks in our guide, and the starting weight is over 24 pounds.

This is a solid choice if you’re a kettlebell athlete or want a heavier adjustable kettlebell (and you’re okay with the adjustment process).

From the company that brought adjustable dumbbells into the mainstream, BowFlex’s SelectTech 840 adjustable kettlebell is a great entry-level model for the kettlebell-curious gym-goer. It’s reasonably priced, replaces six kettlebells, and adjusts easily on the fly. The SelectTech 840 offers six different weights: Eight, 12, 20, 25, 35, and 40 pounds, enough weight to challenge you during isolation movements like curls and extensions while providing enough resistance for snatches, cleans, and rows.

If you’ve been training with kettlebells for a few years, 40 pounds will likely be too light, so you’ll want a kettlebell with a heavier top-end weight or consider buying two of this model. While it isn’t shaped exactly like a kettlebell, it feels enough like one that anyone who uses a traditional kettlebell won’t be completely thrown off. The dial on top of the kettlebell makes adjusting between weights a breeze, and the wide handle makes two-handed exercises easier.

I don’t love the plastic shell, which leaves the SelectTech 840 more prone to breaking if dropped. Also, the smooth handle makes it harder to hold onto the bell, especially after you’ve worked up a sweat. Overall, this is a basic, easy-to-use kettlebell with a moderately challenging weight range. If you’re a beginner or casual kettlebell user, you’ll enjoy BowFlex’s adjustable kettlebell.

Powerblock is best known for its rectangular adjustable dumbbells, which can hold up to 100 pounds, but the brand also makes a rugged, compact adjustable kettlebell with a decent weight range.

The 18- to 35-pound kettlebell measures 5.75″ L x 4.25″ W x 10″ H, while the 35-to-62-pound kettlebell measures 8″ L x 5.5″ W x 11.25″ H. That’s not drastically smaller than other kettlebells in our guide—in fact, Titan’s adjustable kettlebell is half an inch shorter than Powerblock’s heavier kettlebell—but its size relative to the weight range earned it the superlative of most compact.

We like a few things about this kettlebell. First, the handle is wider than most single-weight and adjustable kettlebells, which I like for two-handed movements like swings and upright rows. This kettlebell is also made from steel and feels sturdy and durable. You can drop it without worrying it will break; there aren’t any plastic parts. Lastly, the untraditional shape may throw off some kettlebell enthusiasts, but I think the sloped sides make it sit more comfortably on my wrist. Anyone who snatched or cleaned a traditional kettlebell knows the pressure that can be put on the wrist.

Unfortunately, you have to choose between a lighter or heavier kettlebell. Each model replaces just four kettlebells, less than any other pick here. With either kettlebell, you’ll get the shell plus three weights you can select with a pin. (FYI: You need the pin to choose the weights, and Powerblock doesn’t seem to sell a replacement part.) Sixty-two pounds is a substantial top-end weight for an adjustable kettlebell, and only the Titan Loadable Kettlebell Swing and Bells of Steel Competition Kettlebell offer a heavier option.

We picked Titan as the best budget option because, for this price, the equivalent of seven kettlebells is a pretty damn good deal. It looks and (mostly) feels like a traditional kettlebell, is compact, and uses cast-iron plates, which adds to the product’s durability. What we like most about Titan’s kettlebell is its price and shape. Regarding gym equipment, this is pretty affordable for almost any product. A 40-pound kettlebell from Titan Fitness is no small cost, so add six more kettlebells to your cart; it is worth it.

The shape and size are comparable to traditional kettlebells, so you shouldn’t have a hard time adjusting your technique if you switch to this model. This kettlebell starts at 10 pounds and goes up to 40 pounds, a good weight range for beginners and intermediate lifters. The weight is light enough to master movements like the snatch, clean, and jerk and to burn out the muscles during exercises like curls and overhead presses.

Unfortunately, 40 pounds isn’t enough weight for stronger individuals to get much out of movements like kettlebell swings, rows, chest presses, and deadlifts. If you want to do high-rep workouts with intensity, you can still use this bell. However, expect to outgrow this weight range at some point.

The weights on this kettlebell aren’t marked, so you need to read the plates on the inside to figure out how much you’re lifting. Ideally, Titan would paint the numbers somewhere on this kettlebell. Also, adjusting Titan’s kettlebell isn’t as easy as most other picks we've tested. You need to unlock the plates and then slide them out one at a time. But these are little nuisances in the grander scheme of what you're getting for the price.

We’ll admit that this is more of a kettlebell-adjacent tool, but we're including it because it’s affordable, you can load it up to 500 pounds, it uses weight plates, and you can use it in a few creative ways.

First, let’s be clear: Titan’s loadable handle is not a kettlebell replacement. It’s nowhere near the size of a standard kettlebell, so you can’t perform classic kettlebell movements like the snatch, clean, and jerk. As the name implies, Titan’s Loadable Kettlebell Swing is for swinging, with the main benefit being that you can load it with hundreds of pounds.

Swinging this handle will not feel like swinging a kettlebell. It’s 19 inches tall, eight inches taller than a competition kettlebell. You’ll probably feel unstable and unbalanced the first few times you swing it, since the plates are relatively far from your center of gravity. You’ll also need to assume a wider stance than you do with standard kettlebells. A competition kettlebell is 8.25 inches wide. By comparison, some metal 45-pound plates are nearly 17 inches across, and 25-pound plates are almost 12 inches across. We suggest loading 5-, 10-, and 25-pound plates onto the handle so you don’t have to widen your stance.

Even though you can’t technically replace a kettlebell with this handle, it’s still a valuable and fun addition to any home gym. Aside from heavy swings, you can perform one-arm rows, upright rows, single-arm farmer’s carries, duck walks, and elevated sumo deadlifts with this handle. We say “addition” to a home gym because this handle is an excellent buy if you own weight plates. Otherwise, you’ll need to shell out extra money for plates to load it.

If you’re looking for a pure kettlebell replacement, Titan’s Loadable Kettlebell Swing is not for you. However, with this price tag and a 500-pound weight capacity, we think serious strength athletes will love this unique tool for heavy swings, rows, elevated deadlifts, and carries.

Most adjustable kettlebells range from 10 to 40 pounds. We looked for brands that offer either a wider range of weights in one kettlebell or multiple kettlebells with different weight ranges.

For movements like swings, deadlifts, rows, and push presses, anything under 40 pounds is too light to challenge anyone who isn’t a beginner. Ten to 30 pounds is great for isolation exercises (think curls, lateral raises, and extensions), but it won’t properly challenge the explosive movements people expect to do with kettlebells.

The handle needs to be easy to grip, comfortable, and able to fit both hands for a variety of exercises. Handle size refers to both the diameter (measured in millimeters) and the width of the handle. A competition-grade kettlebell has a handle diameter of 190mm (or 7.5 inches). Unless you’re training specifically for kettlebell sport, you don’t need to worry about buying a kettlebell with those specific dimensions.

In fact, some of our testers prefer handles that are thinner in diameter (easier to grip) and longer (so you can grab it with both hands). That said, all the kettlebells in this guide are comfortable and effective, and within millimeters of competition-grade specs.

You want an adjustable kettlebell to look and function like a traditional kettlebell, so we mostly chose products that resemble single-weight kettlebells. That said, if a pick in this guide strays from the traditional shape, it’s because we still found it comfortable and/or easy to use.

You’re going to run into a handful of different changing mechanisms for the kettlebells below. The two most common are a dial and pin. For the dial, the kettlebell usually sits on top of a stack of plates. You turn the dial to the weight you want, and the mechanism automatically engages the appropriate number of weight plates. To use the pin, you’ll manually insert it into different holes in the kettlebell that correlate to a specific weight (it’s no different than using a weight stack at the gym). Both dials and pins are quick and efficient mechanisms.

Dials are often made of plastic, so they can break, but in our experience this is rare and unlikely as long as you use your kettlebell sensibly. Competition-style kettlebells may require you to ratchet open the bell with a wrench and manually add or remove metal plate weights before closing it back up. This is a pain, but the trade-off is more stability and durability, and an adjustable kettlebell that’s shaped like and performs like a traditional one. Kettlebell handles aren’t really kettlebells, but handles with an extended pole for you to load weights onto. This process shouldn’t feel too different from loading a barbell.
