#4783. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4781. Pornography Perception: Shame Intensifies Distress Over Use

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

How much pornography is too much? People often assume that the more someone watches, the more likely they are to develop an escalating, progressive addiction.

A new study by psychologist Joshua Grubbs and colleagues complicates that story. Their findings suggest that understanding perceived problematic pornography use requires looking beyond frequency to people’s beliefs about what they are doing. The researchers also found that periods of unusually high perceived problems tended to be followed by a return toward the person’s usual level, challenging assumptions of inevitable worsening.

Published in the flagship Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science, the study followed American adults across five assessments over two years. Its analyses included 2,903 people who reported pornography use during at least one assessment.

Researchers measured how frequently participants watched pornography, how strongly they morally disapproved of it, and their self-reported problematic pornography use, or PPU. That last measure assessed experiences such as feeling unable to stop using pornography. It measured perceived problems rather than establishing a clinical diagnosis.

The central concept was moral incongruence: the shame and conflict people experience when their behavior violates their values. Someone who believes pornography is wrong but continues watching it may experience distress and interpret their distress over doing something they regret as evidence of addiction.

The researchers examined both differences between people and changes within the same person. That distinction matters. Asking whether frequent viewers report more problems than occasional viewers is different from asking whether someone feels more troubled during periods when they watch more than usual.

People who morally disapproved of pornography generally watched it less often. Among those who watched porn, however, greater moral disapproval was associated with more perceived problems.

Moral disapproval also amplified the relationship between viewing frequency and perceived problems. When participants watched more than their own usual amount, the association with perceived problems was roughly three times stronger among people with high moral disapproval than among those with low disapproval.

As Grubbs explained in an emailed statement about the findings:

“It's not just that people who disapprove of pornography more are more likely to interpret their own use as problematic; it's that people interpret fluctuations in their own use in light of those deeply held moral beliefs.”

Imagine two people who each increase their viewing by a similar amount. Someone who regards pornography as acceptable might experience little additional concern. Someone who believes it is morally wrong might interpret that increase as evidence of losing control.

An important qualification: the study did not find that frequency mattered only when moral incongruence was present. The association remained positive at lower levels of moral disapproval. The finding was that underlying moral disapproval substantially strengthened that relationship.

The broader message remains consequential: frequency alone cannot tell us whether someone has a pornography problem. The meaning people attach to their behavior helps shape how problematic it feels.

Because this was an observational study, it cannot prove that moral beliefs caused the reported problems. It does show why simply counting viewing occasions provides an incomplete picture.

Another finding challenges a familiar narrative: that pornography problems necessarily become progressively worse.

When participants reported PPU above their own usual level, they tended to report relatively lower PPU six months later. The researchers described this as regression toward the mean.

In everyday language, an unusually bad period tended to be followed by a less extreme one, probably because men often increase use of porn when they are struggling emotionally due to life events, and such life events often subside or lessen over time.

Likewise, watching more pornography than usual at one assessment did not reliably predict greater perceived problems six months later. The relationship between increased viewing and increased concern appeared primarily at the same assessment, rather than demonstrating a clear chain of future deterioration.

These findings are inconsistent with a simple story in which every increase in viewing signals a progressive downward spiral.

They also require careful interpretation. Returning toward one’s usual level does not necessarily mean the person has no struggles with pornography use. Someone’s usual level may still involve considerable distress. Overall differences between people were fairly stable, and the study did not establish that everyone improved or that persistent problems resolve without help.

This was also a community sample, rather than a study specifically of patients seeking treatment. Its findings cannot determine the course of every severe clinical case.

Still, a temporary spike in perceived problems should not automatically be treated as evidence of an escalating disorder.

People distressed about pornography deserve to have that distress taken seriously. Understanding its source is essential.

A useful assessment explores whether someone is experiencing persistent difficulty controlling their behavior, concrete consequences, conflict with personal values, or some combination. Moral conflict and difficulties with control can coexist.

Addressing distress rooted in moral incongruence should respect the person’s values while helping them examine shame and frightening interpretations of their behavior. Assuming that every unwanted viewing episode proves addiction risks reinforcing the very distress bringing someone into treatment.

This research encourages a more careful question than “How often do you watch?”

Instead, let's ask: What happens in your life when you watch—and what does watching porn mean to you?

Reference: Grubbs, J. B., Floyd, C. G., Carrasquillo, K. D., & Kraus, S. W. (2026). The dual-level dynamics of moral incongruence: A multilevel analysis of problematic pornography use. Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science. Advance online publication.

#4780. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4779. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4778. Cancer Taught Dolph Lundgren He’s Not Invincible. Now He’s Finding New Strength.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

After three years with no evidence of disease, the action legend is training smarter—and living differently.

DOLPH LUNDGREN HAS had one hell of a life. From being plucked from obscurity into a modeling career after studying chemical engineering at MIT, to dating Grace Jones, to becoming one of the iconic bad guys of the 1980s, what hasn’t he done? Just one of those things would be a highlight in anybody’s life. But Dolph Lundgren isn’t just anybody.

Seemingly cut from stone and delivered to America ready-made to star in films, his path upon arrival from Sweden wasn’t always easy. In the new documentary, Dolph: Unbreakable, Lundgren gets candid about a childhood of abuse and the struggle to put that behind him. He also discusses the films he felt didn’t meet his standards after he was established as a household name thanks to roles in Rocky IV, Universal Soldier, and Masters of the Universe. While there are certainly gems to be discovered in that direct-to-video period, it's fascinating to watch the man many know as Ivan Drago, a brute with few words, open up about his life and career. Perhaps the film’s biggest revelation is that of Lundgren’s fight with cancer, a diagnosis that, at one point, gave him just a few months to live.

That fight scaffolds Dolph: Unbreakable, and it’s moving to watch a man so seemingly superhuman allow himself to be so vulnerable. Now, on the other side of that battle and going strong, Lundgren is out in the world touring with his new memoir, Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle, alongside the doc. Taking a moment from his busy schedule, the 69-year-old legend sat down with Men’s Health to discuss his new fitness app, Brandon Lee and learning from Sylvester Stallone.

MEN’S HEALTH: How’s your health these days?

DOLPH LUNDGREN: It's good, man. It's good. I've been NED—no evidence of disease—for three years now. I'm doing a scan every couple of months. I mean, I still work out. I work out a lot now, actually, like I used to. I’m feeling great. I'm working on a fitness app—My friend Arnold has one. I'm going to do a much smaller personal one about exactly how I work out; It's more confined to what I do.

But physically, I feel good. Psychologically, once you have the cancer diagnosis, you're always wondering what's going to come in the future, but it keeps you honest on some level. It keeps me honest about enjoying the moments.

MH: Even in the scariest moments of your diagnosis in the documentary, you always looked like you were in great shape. How has your approach to fitness evolved as you’ve gotten older?

DL: It's gotten a little more focused. As you get older, you have more responsibilities and you have less time, especially these days with all the digital noise in the world. I think I’ve also gotten a little smarter. The cancer journey made me realize I'm not invincible, and even though I want to do crazy stuff like I used to and spar with 25-year-olds and run up the mountain, I can’t do that anymore.

I said, "No, I'm going to cut back on the crazy stuff." And I've devised this workout schedule that's based on 30- to 40-minute workouts a couple times a week, and I've distilled it down to what I think really works, what doesn't get you injured, and what you have access to. Most people have access to a gym. So, most of it is strength training. There's some cardio involved, plus a little movement and mobility from martial arts. I've come up with a pretty clever and pretty efficient program.

MH: I love how candid you get in the film, especially about your own work. You’re hard on some of your direct-to-video work, but those projects still have a lot of fans. Is there anything you think went under the radar?

DL: Look, what I would say is I'm proud of my own work, but I may not be totally ecstatic about how the films turned out sometimes. I wasn't the director. Some of the movies, however, like Command Performance, I'm very proud of. That's a movie I directed. I think what I said in the doc was that the focus wasn’t necessarily to make a good movie. It was just to make quick money. I definitely feel good about the movies I directed. I feel good about Command Performance and Wanted Man. Movies like I Come in Peace—I know a lot of people like that one. Unfortunately, we couldn’t include that one in the documentary. There’s only so much space. [Laughs] They're all testaments of their time. They may not be prominent, but they've clearly played a part in my life and my development as a person and as an actor.

MH: Showdown in Little Tokyo is an all-time favorite of mine. I love your dynamic in it with Brandon Lee. What are your memories of him?

DL: My main memory of him is that he was a great guy. We really got along very well, both off-screen and on-screen. Obviously, I was a fan of his dad's, Bruce. I think his mom, Linda Lee, was half Swedish. I think her grandmother was from Sweden. He had been to Sweden, and had a quarter of Scandinavian descent. That's why he was tall, and had those good looks—that mix between her and Bruce.

He spoke some Swedish, and we bonded over that. Then, of course, the martial arts: he did the same style as his dad, and I was doing Kyokushin karate, a different style. We had such a great time together. I was very, very upset when I got that call a couple years later that he'd gotten killed in some freak accident. He would've certainly been a huge star.

MH: You were speaking earlier about your development as an actor. You’ve always been a compelling screen presence, but you’ve become better and better as you’ve gotten older. You give incredible performances in movies like Creed II and Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning. What’s it been like to stretch yourself?

DL: It's been great. I remember an interview with Russell Crowe where he was asked, "How do you create a great character?" And he says, "Work with a great director." It's hard to display great acting if you're not working with a great director, because he's the artist. That's why Marlon Brando made bad movies once in a while. He was usually interesting, but maybe the movie was forgettable.

As a martial artist, as an engineer, I was used to being trained from the ground up properly for years. Martial arts took seven years to get a black belt. I started acting when I was 23, and I was thrown into a big movie very quickly. The movie was a hit, and suddenly I'm in Hollywood. I'm now starring in my own movies, but I didn't have much experience. I had to learn on the job, and it wasn't easy. But think about Stallone, for instance. He’d done some great acting, but before that, he was a writer. He wanted to be a star early on. I hadn't even thought of it before Rocky IV. It took me years after that to acquire more confidence and skill.

With recent films, especially Creed II and Aquaman, I had a chance to work with better directors and actors, and play more interesting characters. I still do action stuff and action comedies where it's not as focused, but I do like to apply myself. Now, I'm interested in applying myself, post-cancer, to dramatic roles to see what happens, because I haven't done it yet. It's going to be interesting. I'm doing some of those kinds of movies this year and next year.

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. #4776. The Sadness of Borrowed Dogs

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In Ron Howard’s new documentary Avedon, the internationally renowned photographer Richard Avedon recalls “the sadness of borrowed dogs.” Throughout his childhood, his family borrowed dogs from neighbors to complete the happy family photos.

"We were not satisfied with the way we were,” Avedon says, while reflecting on his sister, Louise, who suffered from mental illness. She was eventually admitted to a psychiatric hospital after becoming increasingly withdrawn from reality due to schizophrenia.

The borrowed dog is a small detail that reveals a larger family dynamic. John Bradshaw called this staged domestic harmony a shame-based family system: a family organized around hiding its defects. In my view, these polished photographs of the happy Avedon family are what shame looks like when an entire family maintains the pretense. The photos show the family as it wants to be seen.

Photographs are one way to keep up appearances. Another way, which is common in families affected by addiction or abuse, is living by three unwritten rules: don’t talk, don’t trust, and don’t feel. Those rules keep the outside image intact. I hear versions of these rules all the time from clients who grew up being told “children should be seen and not heard,” “don’t make waves,” or “keep the peace.”

Children who are exposed to these messages learn to make themselves small to avoid being singled out, perhaps by an alcoholic parent who flies into rages. In that house, shrinking is a survival skill the child learns: their needs don’t matter, and safety depends on staying unseen.

They carry it with them, hiding their defects, and it becomes armor. The armor goes with them when they leave home. Some go on to build successful lives despite this armor. But they do so at a cost: They never let themselves live an authentic life, because if the armor slipped for even a second, someone might see them. And that feels dangerous.

Avedon’s son says his father adored Louise but never visited her in the institute where she languished. Perhaps Avedon feared finding her somewhere like the hospital he photographed in 1963. That February, he spent time at the East Louisiana State Mental Hospital and made his Mental Institution series. This unflinching set of pictures was meant to support that year's mental health reform movement. When they appeared in Nothing Personal, his 1964 book with James Baldwin, the critic Robert Brustein accused Avedon of offering “a titillating peek into the obscene and ugly faces of the mad.”

Unlike Brustein, who saw exploitation, I see the borrowed-dog snapshot turned inside out. The family album hid Louise’s illness, and the asylum photographs refused to look away from it. Avedon’s career is proof of that refusal.

As a child, Avedon posed with a borrowed dog. As an adult, he spent his career photographing everything his family had taught him to hide, except the one person he couldn’t bear to visit.

Avedon, R., & Baldwin, J. (1964). Nothing Personal. Atheneum.

Black, C. (1981). It Will Never Happen to Me! Children of Alcoholics: As Youngsters, Adolescents, Adults. M.A.C. Printing and Publications.

Bradshaw, J. (1988). Healing the Shame That Binds You. Health Communications.

Howard, R. (Director). (2026). Avedon [Documentary film]. Imagine Documentaries; Fifth Season; Netflix.

Richard Avedon Foundation. (n.d.). Mental Institution, East Louisiana State Mental Hospital, Jackson, Louisiana, February 1963 [Photograph series]. https://avedonfoundation.org/the-work

#4775. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4774. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4773. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4772. Can AI Really Make Us Feel Seen?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

MIT professor Sherry Turkle’s new book Artificial Intimacy explores what happens when people turn to chatbots for the kind of understanding we used to seek from each other.

In one exchange she describes, a man asks his chatbot whether his former girlfriend was right that he was emotionally unavailable. He brings a painful judgment about himself to a machine that is likely to offer a fluent, sympathetic response, instead of asking another person whose reply might be more unpredictable.

Turkle has studied our relationships with technology for decades

Today people use chatbots as companions, therapists, confidants, and romantic partners. “Pretend empathy" is the term Turkle uses to describe the sympathetic replies of the chatbots. Through her own experiments, she acknowledges just how powerful their responses can feel. She argues that because talking to a chatbot feels so easy, people may come to prefer it to human relationships, which take more work and can sometimes be uncomfortable.

Most people like hearing that their reactions make sense, especially when they are upset or hurt. It's harder to hear that we contributed to a problem, misunderstood something, or missed what someone else was trying to tell us. Another person who knows us may notice a pattern we have missed or remember an encounter differently. It can be unsettling to be shown something about ourselves that we couldn't see for ourselves. We often learn more about ourselves from knowing how our words and actions landed with someone else.

A chatbot's reassurance can soothe us when we are upset while leaving our account of events unchallenged. Validating a person's feelings doesn’t necessarily mean endorsing their version of what happened. But with a sympathetic reply, the two can easily blur. That's what’s called the sycophantic pull. This is when the chatbot’s agreement feels like insight, even when the response only reinforces the user's version of events. This helps explain the preference that Turkle describes. Of course, we want to return to the listener who always seems to agree with us.

One thing that can make the pull even stronger is that the chatbot can sound like an objective observer. But the chatbot knows only what we tell it. For instance, when we describe an argument, we choose the details and frame what happened, and the chatbot works only from the information we provided it with.

A therapist also starts with one person's account, but then brings independent judgment and experience to it. A therapist or confidant may notice what we leave out or question how we tell our story. A chatbot's polished answer can sound like a second opinion, but it’s really just our own account handed back to us in more confident language.

There is also a difference in who has to live with the consequences of the advice given.

A chatbot's sympathetic replies can sound like concern, but the program has no feelings about us and won't be affected by the outcome.

If the man acts on its answer, whether by reaching out to his former girlfriend or by deciding she was wrong about him, the chatbot won’t wonder how things turned out or bear any responsibility for the outcome. Professional ethics guide therapists. A friend has lived with the advice they gave, and with us, afterward.

When someone who has to face us afterward tells us something we don't want to hear, they are risking their relationship with us to say it. But a chatbot's agreement costs it nothing. That’s why the difficulty and awkwardness of human relationships is so essential. Another person may see us differently from how we see ourselves. If we turn to a chatbot's soothing agreement instead of risking disagreement and repair in real relationships, we miss chances to see our behavior from another’s perspective.

I explore these ideas in my forthcoming book, Being Seen: The Psychology of Visibility – Its Promise and Peril. Other people can help us recognize parts of ourselves that we can’t see for ourselves. Another person’s view can be painful or mistaken, but it comes from someone with an independent mind and one who cares what happens to us. A chatbot can soothe us with an answer that feels personal, but it has no independent point of view from what we tell it and nothing to lose if its advice goes wrong.

#4771. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

#4769. Music as an Intervention in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Music has long been part of ceremonial and healing practices involving psychedelics, and it has played a role in Western psychedelic research for decades. But as researchers learn more about how music influences patients during psychedelic-assisted therapy, an important idea is emerging: Music isn't simply something playing in the background. It is part of the therapeutic intervention itself. However, a recent 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical Psychology highlighted how little data has been gathered to date about the role of music in psychedelic clinical trials.

In psychedelic-assisted therapy, set and setting are at the core of the process. Set refers to the patient's mindset, expectations, and emotional state, while setting encompasses the physical, social, and therapeutic environment in which treatment takes place.

Music is an important part of that setting. Early psychedelic research sometimes involved sessions conducted in relatively sterile environments with little sensory stimulation. Over time, researchers and therapists came to recognize the importance of creating a more supportive environment, including the use of music. Even the absence of music could create a response.

One of music's most valuable functions is that it provides a sense of movement throughout a dosing session. A piece of music begins, develops, and eventually ends. Another takes its place. The emotional tone, rhythm, and instrumentation change, offering patients a reminder that whatever they are experiencing in the moment will also change.

A 2026 review published in Brain and Behavior suggested that music can intensify emotions, influence brain networks involved in meaning and imagery, and affect patterns of brain activity during psychedelic states. However, the researchers also emphasized that the evidence remains limited.

One of the challenges in selecting music for psychedelic-assisted therapy is that no two people hear music in exactly the same way. A piece of classical music might evoke peace for one person and sadness for another. Choral music may feel deeply meaningful to someone with a spiritual background but uncomfortable to someone whose religious experiences have been painful. Even a particular instrument can carry strong personal associations. For this reason, it is virtually impossible to choose music that is completely "neutral."

Every musical selection has the potential to influence a patient's experience, whether through its emotional qualities, cultural associations, or personal significance. This doesn't mean that every piece of music will have a profound effect. Some patients may barely notice what is playing, while others may find the music central to their experience.

A 2018 study published in Psychopharmacology, titled "The Hidden Therapist," examined patients receiving psilocybin treatment for depression. Researchers found that patients' responses to music, particularly their sense of resonance with it, were associated with aspects of their psychedelic therapy experience and changes in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that how patients relate to the music may matter as much as the music itself.

One of the more interesting aspects of music in psychedelic-assisted therapy is that patients are not encouraged to avoid every uncomfortable response. In preparation sessions, therapists may discuss what to do if a patient encounters music they dislike or find emotionally challenging. For example, if a song brings up sadness, a patient might be encouraged to notice what is happening and consider whether they can remain with the feeling for a short time rather than immediately trying to escape it.

Even the experience of disliking a piece of music can offer an opportunity for observation. What happens when something feels unpleasant? What thoughts, sensations, or emotions arise? Is it possible to experience discomfort without immediately needing to change it? These questions connect to a broader principle of psychedelic-assisted therapy: learning to approach difficult emotions with curiosity rather than automatic avoidance.

But there is an important distinction between allowing space for discomfort and imposing it.

If music becomes overwhelming, distressing, or simply feels inappropriate for the moment, patients should be able to communicate that to their therapists. Depending on the research protocol, the music may be changed, skipped, lowered in volume, or temporarily turned off.

Patient autonomy remains essential. Music may be part of the therapeutic intervention, but patients should understand their options and have opportunities to express their preferences and concerns.

Music's role in psychedelic-assisted therapy may continue after the effects of the medication have subsided. Integration is the phase of treatment in which patients reflect on their experiences, explore their meaning, and consider how to apply insights to everyday life.

For some patients, listening to music from their dosing session can help them reconnect with emotions, memories, or perspectives that emerged during treatment. Sometimes, playlists are made available to participants after their dosing session. Some have reported returning to the music during quiet reflection, while others listen during ordinary activities such as gardening or getting ready for the day.

For certain patients, the music becomes a meaningful reminder of their therapeutic experience, sometimes years later. What such experiences suggest is that music may provide a connection between the dosing session and the ongoing work of therapy.

The compound is only one part of psychedelic-assisted therapy. The therapeutic relationship, preparation, environment, integration, and music all help shape the patient's experience.

Music may offer comfort, evoke memories, or help patients navigate difficult emotions. At times, silence may be more appropriate. What matters is not simply what is played but how each patient responds. By approaching music with intention and flexibility, therapists can make it a meaningful part of individualized care

Jess M. Jones, LCSWC, holds a B.A. in sociology from Wesleyan University, an M.S.W. from the University of Pennsylvania, and multiple clinical certifications in psychedelic-assisted therapy. She has specialized training in MDMA-and ketamine-assisted therapy and also serves as a trainer and mentor with Fluence.

#4767. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4766. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4765. Why Shame Matters in Politics

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In the November 2026 American midterm elections, campaign advertisements were relentless. Across broadcast television and digital media, a record 573.2 and 500 million dollars were spent on Texas and Ohio campaigns, respectively.[1] Americans received a combined 60 billion political text messages, an average of 170 messages per person.[2]

The quantity of messages was startling, but so was their content, which frequently transgressed the bounds of decorum. Many campaigns involved insults and unsubstantiated rumors, meant to undermine the credibility of candidates.[3] These were cases of mudslinging—the exchange of personal insults or abuse, especially unjust ones, to damage the reputation of an opponent.[4] While the delivery of unsolicited messages directly to our iPhones was a novel experience, mudslinging itself is not a new American phenomenon.

For example, in the 1796 U.S. presidential election, John Adams and his supporters called Thomas Jefferson an atheist, and Jefferson’s supporters referred to Adams as “His Rotundity” and an “old, querulous, bald, crippled, toothless Adams.”[5] In the presidential election of 1828, Democrats accused John Quincy Adams of the misuse of public funds, and Whigs attacked Andrew Jackson’s military record and character.[6]

There are helpful ways to criticize a political opponent in an election. Examples include drawing attention to a poor track record of leadership or patterns of equivocation in policy statements. But personal vitriol, fabricated attacks, and ridicule are not among them. Mudslinging is often at odds with virtues such as charity and honesty. It distracts from substantive policy conversations. When a candidate campaigns in this way, he has shown himself to be undiscerning, cruel, and sometimes shameless.

To be shameless is to avoid moral censure or be unapologetic in wrongdoing. The shameless person intentionally flouts moral norms—doing the wrong thing, even though he knows better. Alternatively, he may be unaware of moral norms—even though he should have known better. In either case, the shameless person is blameworthy yet fails to experience the sting of a moral sanction.

I provided a recent example of shamelessness in American civic life—campaigns built around dishonesty and personal vitriol. But shamelessness is not just a problem during election cycles. It is a problem in daily governance, such as when leaders demean others or abuse power for personal gain. It is a problem on social media, where people overshare personal information and make inappropriate jokes. And shamelessness is a problem in corporate America. Examples include fraud, bribery, and flagrant violations of environmental protections.

So, why does shame matter in politics? Here are three reasons.

Shame is a negative-valence, self-conscious emotion, characterized by a critical self-evaluation.[7] It construes oneself as problematic. Shame is not an emotion that people like to experience. It is popularly regarded as “guilt’s ugly sister” and a disposable emotion.[8] We would rather do away with shame entirely than feel bad about ourselves. However, it is probably not a coincidence that a culture that wishes to dispose of shame is also riddled with shamelessness. If we are not sensitive to wrongdoing, how can we be expected to act well?

A better (albeit more challenging) approach is to recover shame in healthy forms. This is the approach we take with other misdirected emotions. An example is that, when a child throws a tantrum, we do not regard her anger as disposable or inherently unproductive. We educate this emotion toward its proper end, helping the child to experience anger in fitting ways.

I defined shame in terms of a global negative self-evaluation. This distinguishes shame from guilt, which attends to particular bad actions. Tangney (1998) puts it this way: Shame says, “I did that terrible thing,” whereas guilt says, “I did that terrible thing.” In some cases, shame’s self-evaluation makes it less action-guiding, since shame, unlike guilt, does not see a particular wrongdoing to repair. However, shame’s construal of the person means the emotion can better recognize patterns of bad action.

Additionally, shame attends to considerations of moral beauty or fineness—features of the moral life which are not neatly captured in terms of ‘good’ and ‘bad’.[9] Finally, shame attends to social standing and relational repair.[10] It aids our sensitivity to the feelings and expectations of others. Without shame, we lack the vision it provides, which helps us navigate the complexities of the moral life.

Imagine you have a rule in your home: no jumping on the couches. But you don’t enforce the rule. Maybe you see the child jumping, and instead of scolding him, you turn away or smile. The child may jump on the couch tentatively at first. Eventually he will jump freely and shamelessly, unconcerned about the rule that apparently does not apply to him.

Shame matters because it holds a leader to a standard and keeps the standard emotionally salient. This is important because it reduces the likelihood of bad actions. It also reduces the tendency toward assumptions of norm-differentiation in leadership—acting as though rules, in general, do not apply.

Finally, shame matters because we are imitative creatures. We can tell young people that moral character matters, but when those in authority are uncivil and unapologetic, or shameless in how they comport themselves in public, this is the lesson that stays with them.

[1] Mort, E. 2026. $573M: Most Expensive Non-Presidential Race on Record. AdImpact.

[2] Meyer, M. 2026. Stop Those Aggravating Midterm Election Political Text Messages. CNET.

[3] Schwenk, K. Sep. 14, 2026. Cruz-Linked PAC Targets El-Sayed In “Death To America” Ad. The Lever; AP. Oct. 29, 2026. Controversial attack ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother has run its course in Ohio. 10 WBNS.

[5] Goodtimes, J. 2012. A brief history of campaign mudslinging from 1796 to today. Philadelphia Magazine.

[6] Hansen, W. Campaign Mudslinging: An American Tradition since (at Least) 1828. The Newberry.

[7] Tangney, J.P. 1998. How Does Guilt Differ from Shame? In Guilt and Children, ed. J. Bybee, 1–17. Cambridge. Little, S. 2023. A Case for Shame in Character Education. Studies in Philosophy and Education. 42: 283–302.

[8] Kristjánsson, K. 2014. Is shame an ugly emotion? Four discourses—Two contrasting interpretations for moral education. Studies in Philosophy and Education 33: 495–511.

[9] Jimenez, M. 2020. Aristotle on Shame and Learning to Be Good. Oxford University Press.

[10] Calhoun, Cheshire. 2004. “An Apology for Moral Shame.” Journal of Political Philosophy 12 (2): 127–244.
